subject: math
title: Number Sense: Integers, Order of Operations, Fractions, and Decimals
objectives: You will locate, compare, and order integers, fractions, and decimals on a number line, and find absolute value.
You will add, subtract, multiply, and divide positive and negative numbers using the sign rules.
You will evaluate expressions with the correct order of operations, including grouping symbols and absolute value bars.
You will add, subtract, multiply, and divide fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals, and convert between fractions and decimals.
You will solve multi-step word problems involving money, temperature, and measurement.

slides.title: Week 1 Math: Number Sense
slides.board:
Number Sense

Integers, Order of Operations, Fractions, and Decimals

  • Compare and order numbers; find absolute value
  • Compute with positive and negative numbers
  • Use the order of operations
  • Compute with fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals
  • Solve multi-step word problems

Today: warm-up, signed numbers, order of operations, fractions, decimals, word problems, GED-style questions

notes.say: Welcome to Week 1. Everything on the GED math test sits on top of today's skills: if your signs, your order of steps, and your fractions are solid, algebra and geometry get much easier later. The first part of the GED math test does not allow a calculator, so today we work by hand and write every step. Here is how today works: I explain a rule, I show you a worked example, we do some together, and then you try some on your own while I watch the clock.
ask: On a scale of 1 to 5, how comfortable are you with negative numbers? With fractions? (expected answer: any; use it to decide where to slow down)
notes.watch: Pacing for 60 minutes: warm-up 5 min (slide 2); signed numbers 12 min (slides 3–9); order of operations 12 min (slides 10–14); fractions 11 min (slides 15–19); decimals 8 min (slides 20–23); word problems 9 min (slides 24–26); strategy and recap 3 min (slides 27–28). If you fall behind, shorten the we-do slides to two problems each.

slides.title: Warm-up: What Do You Remember?
slides.board:
Work these on paper. No calculator.

  1. −4 + 9
  2. 3 − 10
  3. 1/2 + 1/4
  4. 0.5 + 0.25
  5. Which is greater, −2 or −5?
steps: 1. −4 + 9 = 5 (start at −4 and move 9 to the right)
2. 3 − 10 = −7 (start at 3 and move 10 to the left)
5. −2 is greater. It is farther right on the number line: −2° is warmer than −5°.

notes.say: This is a check on what you remember, not a grade. Take about three minutes, then tell me your answers one at a time. Notice that problems 3 and 4 are the same amount written two ways, 3/4 and 0.75. Connecting fractions and decimals is a big part of today.
ask: What did you get for number 5, and how did you decide? (expected answer: −2, because it is closer to zero, farther right, or warmer)
notes.watch: Number 5 is the one adults miss most: they pick −5 because 5 is bigger than 2. If that happens, ask "Which is colder, −2° or −5°?" and use it to launch the number line on the next slide. If the student answers 2/6 on number 3, note it; we fix adding denominators on slide 15.

slides.title: The Number Line and Absolute Value
slides.board:
−5−4−3−2−1012345

← less     greater →

  • Integers: whole numbers and their opposites. 0 is neither positive nor negative.
  • Farther right means greater: −2 > −5.
  • Absolute value is distance from 0, never negative: |−6| = 6 and |6| = 6.
  • Opposites are the same distance from 0: 4 and −4. Also −(−4) = 4.

notes.say: Picture a thermometer lying on its side. Numbers grow as you move right and shrink as you move left, so a negative number with a big digit, like −9, is actually very small: it is far below zero. Absolute value asks only "how far from zero?" and not "which direction?", so it is never negative. The bars | | also work like parentheses, which matters later today.
ask: Which is greater, −10 or −2? Why? (expected answer: −2; it is farther right, closer to zero, or warmer)
What is |−15|? (expected answer: 15)
What is the opposite of −7? (expected answer: 7)
notes.watch: Students often think absolute value "makes everything positive" and apply it before working inside the bars. Plant the seed now: |3 − 11| means do 3 − 11 first, then take the distance from zero, so it is 8, not 14.

slides.title: Compare and Order Integers
slides.board:
Order from least to greatest:

3,   −8,   0,   −2,   |−5|,   −(−6)

Method: simplify any absolute values and opposites first, then place every number on one number line.
steps: Rewrite the special forms first: |−5| = 5 and −(−6) = 6.
Now the list is 3, −8, 0, −2, 5, 6. The negatives go on the left side of zero.
Between the negatives, −8 is farther from zero, so −8 < −2.
Check with temperatures: −8° is colder than −2°, which is colder than 0°.

notes.say: When a list mixes forms, clean it up first. Absolute value bars and a negative sign in front of parentheses are instructions: carry them out, then compare. Then put every number on one number line in your head and read it from left to right.
ask: Where does |−5| go, left or right of 0? (expected answer: right; it equals 5)
notes.watch: Watch for a student who places |−5| with the negatives. Ask: "How far is −5 from zero?"

slides.title: Adding and Subtracting Signed Numbers
slides.board:
SituationRuleExample
Add, same signsAdd; keep the sign−5 + (−3) = −8
Add, different signsSubtract the absolute values; keep the sign of the larger one−9 + 4 = −5
SubtractAdd the opposite6 − (−2) = 6 + 2 = 8
−3 − 7 = −3 + (−7) = −10

notes.say: Think of money. A negative is a debt and a positive is cash. If you owe 5 dollars and borrow 3 more, you owe 8: that is −5 + (−3) = −8. If you owe 9 and pay back 4, you still owe 5: −9 + 4 = −5. For subtraction, rewrite before you compute: keep the first number, change minus to plus, and change the sign of the second number. Then use the adding rules.
ask: What is −6 + 10? (expected answer: 4)
Rewrite 2 − (−8) as an addition problem. (expected answer: 2 + 8, which is 10)
notes.watch: The most common error is 5 − (−3) = 2. Have the student say "add the opposite" out loud and rewrite the problem before computing.

slides.title: Temperature Change
slides.board:
At 5 a.m. the temperature was −7°F. By 3 p.m. it was 12°F.

(a) How many degrees did the temperature rise?

(b) By 11 p.m. it had dropped 15 degrees from the 3 p.m. temperature. What was the temperature at 11 p.m.?
steps: Check on the number line: from −7 up to 0 is 7 degrees, and from 0 up to 12 is 12 more. 7 + 12 = 19.
Sense check: dropping 15 degrees from 12 passes zero, so the answer must be negative.

notes.say: Two kinds of temperature questions show up on the GED: "How much did it change?" and "What is it now?" For a change, always compute final minus start, even when the start is negative. For "what is it now," start where you are and move: a rise adds and a drop subtracts.
ask: Why is the rise 19 and not 5? (expected answer: from −7 you climb 7 just to reach zero, then 12 more)
notes.watch: A student who answers 5 for part (a) computed 12 − 7. Count the jumps on the number line together.

slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing Signed Numbers
slides.board:
SignsResultExamples
Same signsPositive(−4)(−5) = 20    −24 ÷ (−6) = 4
Different signsNegative(−4)(5) = −20    24 ÷ (−6) = −4

Many factors: count the negatives. An even number of negatives gives a positive; an odd number gives a negative.

(−2)(−3)(−1) = −6 (three negatives)

notes.say: Multiplying and dividing have the simplest sign rules of all: same signs give a positive, different signs give a negative. Do the arithmetic without the signs first, then decide the sign. One warning: these rules are only for multiplying and dividing. Two negatives added together stay negative: −3 + (−4) is −7, not 7.
ask: What is (−6)(−7)? (expected answer: 42)
Is (−1)(−1)(−1)(−1) positive or negative? (expected answer: positive; four negatives is an even number)
notes.watch: Listen for "two negatives make a positive" being used on addition. If you hear it, ask: "Are we multiplying or adding?"

slides.title: Signed Numbers Together
slides.board:
For each problem, name the rule first, then compute.

  1. −15 + 8
  2. −6 − (−10)
  3. (−3)(−2)(−5)
  4. −42 ÷ 7 × (−2)
steps: 1. Different signs: 15 − 8 = 7. The larger absolute value (15) is negative, so the answer is −7.
2. Add the opposite: −6 + 10. Different signs: 10 − 6 = 4, and the larger is positive, so 4.

notes.say: Let's do these together. For each one, tell me which rule you are using before you tell me the number. I will reveal one line at a time so you can check your thinking, not just your answer.
ask: In number 1, which number has the larger absolute value? (expected answer: −15, so the answer is negative)
In number 3, how many negative factors are there? (expected answer: three, an odd number, so the answer is negative)
notes.watch: On number 2, −16 means the student subtracted 10 instead of adding it. On number 4, −12 means the second negative sign was lost.

slides.title: Your Turn: Signed Numbers
slides.board:
Two minutes. Work on paper, then tell me your answers.

  1. −11 − 4
  2. 9 + (−14)
  3. −56 ÷ (−8)
  4. |−3 − 6|

notes.say: Now it is your turn. I am starting the clock for two minutes. Do not worry about speed yet; write the rule you used next to each answer. When time is up, tell me your four answers and I will reveal them.
ask: Read me your four answers. (expected answer: −15, −5, 7, 9)
notes.answer: (1) −11 + (−4) = −15   (2) different signs: 14 − 9 = 5, and the larger is negative, so −5   (3) same signs, so positive: 7   (4) inside first: −3 − 6 = −9, and |−9| = 9
notes.watch: If number 4 comes back as 3, the student did |−3| and |6| separately (6 − 3). Remind them to work inside the bars first. If number 1 comes back as −7 or 7, review "add the opposite."

slides.title: Order of Operations
slides.board:
1. Grouping: ( ), [ ], | |, and fraction bars. Work inside first.
  2. Exponents (Week 3)
  3. Multiply and divide, left to right
  4. Add and subtract, left to right

× and ÷ are partners. + and − are partners. Work partners in the order they appear.

24 ÷ 4 × 3 = 6 × 3 = 18 (not 2)

notes.say: Everyone agrees on this order so that one expression has one answer. Many people learned PEMDAS and think it means multiplication always comes before division and addition always comes before subtraction. That is not the rule. Multiplication and division are partners at the same level, and you do whichever comes first, left to right. The same goes for addition and subtraction. Rewrite the whole expression after each step; one step per line prevents most mistakes.
ask: What is 15 − 3 × 4? (expected answer: 3; multiply first, then 15 − 12)
What is 10 − 4 + 3? (expected answer: 9; left to right, not 10 − 7)
notes.watch: If the student says 48 for 15 − 3 × 4, they worked left to right. If they say 3 for 10 − 4 + 3, they added before subtracting. Both are common GED wrong answers.

slides.title: Order of Operations with Negatives
slides.board:
Evaluate:

7 − 2 × (5 − 9) ÷ 4

Method: rewrite the whole expression after every step, one step per line.
steps: Multiply (it comes first, reading left to right): 2 × (−4) = −8, so 7 − (−8) ÷ 4

notes.say: Watch how I rewrite the whole line every time. The 7 just waits at the front until the multiplying and dividing are done. The most tempting mistake is to do 7 − 2 first because it is on the left, but subtraction waits until all multiplication and division are finished.
ask: What do you get if you wrongly do 7 − 2 first? (expected answer: 5 × (−4) ÷ 4 = −5)
notes.watch: Two errors to listen for: −5 (subtracted 7 − 2 first) and 5 (wrote 7 − 2 at the last step instead of 7 + 2).

slides.title: Order of Operations Together
slides.board:
1. 12 + 8 ÷ 4 − 3 × 2
  2. 24 ÷ 4 × 3 − 5
  3. |−8| − |2 − 6|
  4. 5 − 3(4 − 9)
steps: 3. |−8| = 8. Inside the second bars, 2 − 6 = −4, and |−4| = 4. So 8 − 4 = 4

notes.say: Let's work these together. Before any arithmetic, tell me which operation goes first and why. In number 4, a number written right next to parentheses means multiply.
ask: In number 1, what do we do first? (expected answer: the division 8 ÷ 4 and the multiplication 3 × 2)
In number 4, what does 3(4 − 9) mean? (expected answer: 3 times the value of 4 − 9)
notes.watch: On number 4, students often do 5 − 3 = 2 first and get −10. On number 3, watch for |2 − 6| treated as 2 + 6 = 8, which gives 0.

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Order of Operations
slides.board:
What is the value of the expression?

6 + 18 ÷ (−3) × 2 − (−4)

A. −12    B. −10    C. −2    D. 7
steps: Eliminate A (−12): it comes from working left to right: 6 + 18 = 24, 24 ÷ (−3) = −8, −8 × 2 = −16, −16 + 4 = −12. Addition cannot come before division.
Eliminate D (7): it comes from multiplying (−3) × 2 = −6 before dividing: 18 ÷ (−6) = −3, then 6 − 3 + 4 = 7. Divide and multiply left to right.
Eliminate B (−10): it comes from treating − (−4) as −4: −6 − 4 = −10. Subtracting a negative means adding.

notes.say: This is what a GED question looks like: four choices, and every wrong choice is the answer someone gets from a common mistake. That means finding your answer on the list does not prove you are right. Work it carefully first, then use the wrong choices as a checklist of the traps you avoided.
ask: Which choice did you get, and what was your first step? (expected answer: C, −2; the first step is 18 ÷ (−3) = −6)
notes.watch: If the student picked A, B, or D, read the matching elimination step aloud and have them find the exact line where their work left the correct path.

slides.title: Your Turn: Order of Operations
slides.board:
Three minutes. Rewrite the expression after every step.

  1. 30 − 12 ÷ 3 × 2
  2. 9 − 4 × (2 − 5)
  3. 2|1 − 6| + (−8) ÷ 4

notes.say: Your turn again: three minutes for three problems. Remember the partners rule, and remember that absolute value bars group. When you are done, tell me your answers and the first step you did in each one.
ask: Read me your answers and your first step for each. (expected answer: 22, 21, 8; first steps 12 ÷ 3, then 2 − 5, then 1 − 6)
notes.watch: Common wrong answers: (1) 12 from working left to right, or 28 from multiplying 3 × 2 before dividing; (2) −15 from doing 9 − 4 first, or −3 from computing 9 − 12 at the end; (3) −12 from using −5 instead of |−5|.

slides.title: Fractions: Add and Subtract
slides.board:
• Find a common denominator and rewrite each fraction.
  • Add or subtract the numerators. Keep the denominator.
  • Simplify.

2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12

Never add denominators: 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5. It is 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

Mixed to improper: 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4

notes.say: Fractions can only be added when the pieces are the same size, and that is what a common denominator does. Twelfths plus twelfths gives twelfths, the same way dollars plus dollars gives dollars. The denominator names the size of the piece, so it does not change when you add. If 1/2 + 1/3 were 2/5, adding would leave you with less than the half you started with, which cannot be right.
ask: What common denominator would you use for 3/4 and 1/6? (expected answer: 12)
Write 3 2/5 as an improper fraction. (expected answer: 17/5)
notes.watch: A student who adds denominators needs a picture: half a dollar plus a third of a dollar is about 83 cents, more than half. 2/5 of a dollar is only 40 cents.

slides.title: Subtracting Mixed Numbers
slides.board:
Subtract:

3 1/2 − 1 2/3

Method: change both mixed numbers to improper fractions, find a common denominator, subtract, then change back.
steps: Estimate to check: 3.5 − 1.7 is about 1.8, and 1 5/6 is about 1.83.

notes.say: With mixed numbers, the safest method is to turn everything into improper fractions first. You can also subtract the whole numbers and the fractions separately, but then you must borrow, because 2/3 is bigger than 1/2. People who skip the borrowing subtract the fractions backward and get 2 1/6. Changing to improper fractions avoids that trap completely.
ask: Why can't we just do 3 − 1 and 1/2 − 2/3? (expected answer: 2/3 is larger than 1/2, so we would have to borrow 1 whole)
notes.watch: The trap answer is 2 1/6, from 3 − 1 = 2 and 2/3 − 1/2 = 1/6. Ask the student to estimate: 3 1/2 minus almost 2 must be less than 2.

slides.title: Fractions: Multiply and Divide
slides.board:
• Multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom. No common denominator needed.
    2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2
  • "Of" means multiply: 2/3 of 12 = 2/3 × 12/1 = 24/3 = 8
  • Divide: keep, change, flip.
    3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 3/4 × 8/3 = 24/12 = 2
  • Change mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

notes.say: Multiplying is the easy one: straight across. Dividing asks "How many of these fit into that?" So 3/4 divided by 3/8 asks how many 3/8 pieces fit into 3/4, and since 3/4 is 6/8, the answer is 2. The shortcut is keep the first fraction, change divide to multiply, and flip only the second fraction.
ask: How many quarters are in a half dollar, and what fraction problem is that? (expected answer: 2; 1/2 ÷ 1/4 = 2)
Which fraction do you flip in 5/6 ÷ 2/3? (expected answer: only the second one; 2/3 becomes 3/2)
notes.watch: Watch for flipping the first fraction or both fractions, and for multiplying only the fraction part of a mixed number: 2 1/4 × 2 is 4 1/2, not 2 2/4.

slides.title: Multiplying and Dividing Mixed Numbers
slides.board:
(a) 1 1/2 × 2 2/3

(b) 5/6 ÷ 2/3

Method: change mixed numbers to improper fractions first. To divide, keep, change, flip.
steps: Sense check: 2/3 fits into 5/6 a little more than once, so 1 1/4 makes sense.

notes.say: Here is the mixed number trap: in part (a), many people multiply 1 × 2 = 2 and 1/2 × 2/3 = 1/3 and say 2 1/3. That is wrong because each whole number also multiplies the other fraction. Converting to improper fractions first handles all of it.
ask: Estimate (a): about 1.5 times about 2.7 is about what? (expected answer: about 4)
notes.watch: If the student says 2 1/3 for (a), they multiplied the parts separately. If they say 5/9 for (b), they multiplied without flipping.

slides.title: Fractions Together
slides.board:
First decide: does this operation need a common denominator?

  1. 2/3 + 3/4
  2. 4 1/2 − 2 3/4
  3. 2/5 of 15
  4. 3 ÷ 3/4

notes.say: We will do these together. For each one, the first thing you tell me is which operation it is, because that decides whether you need a common denominator. Adding and subtracting need one; multiplying and dividing do not.
ask: In number 2, why can't we do 4 − 2 and 1/2 − 3/4 without borrowing? (expected answer: 3/4 is larger than 1/2)
In number 4, how do you write 3 as a fraction? (expected answer: 3/1)
notes.watch: On number 1, 5/7 means the student added tops and bottoms. On number 4, 9/4 means they multiplied (3 × 3/4) instead of dividing.

slides.title: Decimals and Conversions
slides.board:
• Add or subtract: line up the decimal points. 20.00 − 9.89 = 10.11
  • Multiply: multiply as whole numbers, then count the decimal places in both factors. 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.06
  • Divide: move the divisor's point to make it whole; move the dividend's point the same way. 4.2 ÷ 0.06 = 420 ÷ 6 = 70
  • Fraction to decimal: top ÷ bottom. 3/8 = 0.375

1/2 = 0.5   1/4 = 0.25   3/4 = 0.75   1/5 = 0.2   1/8 = 0.125   1/3 ≈ 0.333

notes.say: Decimals follow the same place-value rules as money. When you add or subtract, line up the decimal points and fill empty places with zeros. When you multiply, you do not line anything up: multiply as if there were no points, then count. To compare a fraction with a decimal, turn the fraction into a decimal by dividing top by bottom. Memorize the common pairs at the bottom; they save time on the part of the test with no calculator.
ask: What is 0.4 × 0.5? (expected answer: 0.2; 4 × 5 = 20 with two decimal places is 0.20)
Write 3/5 as a decimal. (expected answer: 0.6)
notes.watch: 0.3 × 0.2 = 0.6 is the classic error. Estimation fixes it: 0.2 is one fifth, and one fifth of 0.3 must be smaller than 0.3.

slides.title: Decimals in Context
slides.board:
Rosa buys 12.6 gallons of gas at $3.45 per gallon. She pays with a $50 bill.

(a) What is the total cost?

(b) How much change does she get?
steps: Decimal places: 12.6 has one and 3.45 has two, so the answer has three: 43.470 = $43.47

notes.say: Money problems are the most common place decimals show up on the GED. Estimate first: about 13 gallons at about 3 and a half dollars is about 45 dollars. If your answer were 4.35 or 434.70, the estimate would tell you the decimal point is in the wrong place.
ask: Estimate the total before we compute. (expected answer: about $40 to $45)
notes.watch: In part (b), have the student write 50 as 50.00 so the borrowing across the zeros is visible, then check by adding back: 43.47 + 6.53 = 50.00.

slides.title: Convert, Then Order
slides.board:
Order from least to greatest:

−1.2,   −3/2,   0.8,   3/4

Method: change every fraction to a decimal, then separate the negatives from the positives.
steps: Negatives first. −1.5 is farther from zero than −1.2, so −1.5 < −1.2.

notes.say: When a list mixes fractions and decimals, put everything in one form, usually decimals. Then separate the negatives from the positives. Among the negatives, remember the flip: the bigger the digits, the smaller the number.
ask: Which is greater, −3/5 or −0.5? (expected answer: −0.5, because −3/5 = −0.6 is farther left)
notes.watch: A student who puts −1.2 first is ordering the negatives as if they were positive.

slides.title: Your Turn: Fractions and Decimals
slides.board:
Four minutes. No calculator.

  1. 3/4 + 5/6
  2. 2 1/3 × 3/7
  3. 0.25 × 1.6
  4. Which is greater: 5/8 or 0.6?

notes.say: Last independent round before word problems: four minutes, four problems. Show your conversions. When you tell me your answers, I want to hear the step that got you there.
ask: Read me your answers. (expected answer: 1 7/12, 1, 0.4, and 5/8)
notes.answer: (1) 9/12 + 10/12 = 19/12 = 1 7/12   (2) 7/3 × 3/7 = 21/21 = 1   (3) 25 × 16 = 400 with three decimal places: 0.400 = 0.4   (4) 5/8 = 0.625, which is greater than 0.600
notes.watch: (1) 8/10 means the denominators were added. (2) 2 1/7 comes from multiplying only the fraction part (1/3 × 3/7 = 1/7). (3) 4 or 0.04 means the decimal places were miscounted. (4) A student who says 0.6 may have read 5/8 as 0.58.

slides.title: A Plan for Word Problems
slides.board:
1. Read: What is the question asking for? Underline it.
  2. Plan: List the steps. Rise, gain, deposit → add. Drop, spend, withdraw → subtract. Of, each, per → multiply. Split equally, how many fit → divide.
  3. Compute: one step per line, with labels.
  4. Check: estimate. Does the answer make sense? Did you answer the question that was asked?

notes.say: Most GED math questions are word problems, and most mistakes in word problems are not arithmetic mistakes: they come from answering the wrong question or stopping one step early. That is why the first step is to underline exactly what is being asked. Then plan the steps in words before you compute. Key words help, but read the whole sentence; "how many more" means subtract even though it says "more."
ask: In "Jordan keeps 3/4 of his pay," what operation does "of" signal? (expected answer: multiply)
What is the most common way people lose points on word problems? (expected answer: stopping one step early or answering a different question)
notes.watch: The GED loves answer choices that are one step short: the total cost when the question asks for change, or the amount withheld when it asks for take-home pay. Teach the student to reread the question before choosing.

slides.title: A Multi-Step Word Problem
slides.board: Keisha has $250. She buys 3 shirts at $18.75 each and a pair of shoes for $64.90. Later she returns 1 shirt for a full refund. How much money does she have now?
steps: Plan: find the cost of the shirts, subtract all the purchases, then add back the refund.
Check another way: she kept 2 shirts and the shoes. 2 × $18.75 + $64.90 = $102.40, and $250.00 − $102.40 = $147.60. The answers match.

notes.say: I will think out loud. First I plan the steps in words, then I compute one line at a time with labels so I can find any mistake later. At the end, I check by solving a different way. Two methods that agree are the best evidence you can have.
ask: What would a student get if they forgot the refund? (expected answer: $128.85)
notes.watch: Students sometimes subtract the refund instead of adding it. Ask: "When a store refunds you, does your money go up or down?"

slides.title: GED-Style Question: Word Problem
slides.board:
Ana has 10 yards of fabric. She cuts 3 pieces that are each 2 1/4 yards long. She splits the fabric that is left into 2 equal table runners. How long is each runner?

A. 3 1/4 yd    B. 1 5/8 yd    C. 3 7/8 yd    D. 1 7/8 yd
steps: Eliminate A (3 1/4): that is the fabric left before splitting. The question asks for each runner, so it still has to be divided by 2.
Eliminate C (3 7/8): it comes from subtracting only one piece: 10 − 2 1/4 = 7 3/4, and 7 3/4 ÷ 2 = 3 7/8.
Eliminate D (1 7/8): it comes from multiplying only the whole part, 3 × 2 1/4 as 6 1/4. Then 10 − 6 1/4 = 3 3/4, and 3 3/4 ÷ 2 = 1 7/8.

notes.say: This is a three-step problem, and the wrong choices sit exactly where people stop early or slip. Plan it: total cut, then what is left, then split. Notice that choice A is a real number from the problem; it is the answer to a different question.
ask: What are the three steps? (expected answer: multiply to find the total cut, subtract from 10, divide by 2)
notes.watch: If the student chose A, practice rereading the question after computing: "Did I find the length of each runner?"

slides.title: GED Strategy: Estimate, Check the Sign, Then Choose
slides.board:
1. Estimate first. Round and get a ballpark answer.
  2. Check the sign. Should the answer be positive or negative?
  3. Work it out on your note board, one step per line.
  4. Use the choices as a trap list. Wrong choices come from common mistakes.

Calculator part: on the TI-30XS, enter a negative number with the (−) key, not the subtraction key.

notes.say: Wrong answers on the GED are not random; they are the answers people get from the exact mistakes we practiced today. So an answer that matches a choice is not proof. Ten seconds of estimating and asking "positive or negative?" catches most of these traps. The first part of the math test has no calculator, so these habits are your safety net there. On the calculator part, the TI-30XS has a separate key for a negative sign, and using the subtraction key instead can give an error or a wrong answer.
ask: Before computing −14 + 23 − 17, is the answer positive or negative, and about how big? (expected answer: negative and small, about −8)

screens.title: What You Will Learn
screens.html:
This lesson builds the number skills that every part of the GED math test depends on. Work through one screen at a time. Most screens teach one rule, show a worked example, and end with a quick check you answer before you move on. Keep paper and a pencil next to you and write every step.

By the end, you will be able to:

  • Compare and order integers, fractions, and decimals, and find absolute value.
  • Add, subtract, multiply, and divide positive and negative numbers.
  • Use the order of operations, including grouping symbols and absolute value bars.
  • Compute with fractions, mixed numbers, and decimals, and convert between fractions and decimals.
  • Solve multi-step word problems with money, temperature, and measurement.

Do not use a calculator for this lesson. The first part of the GED math test does not allow one, so build the habit now.

screens.title: Integers and the Number Line
screens.html:
Integers are the whole numbers and their opposites: …, −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, …. Zero is neither positive nor negative.

On a number line, numbers increase as you move right and decrease as you move left. Any number to the right of another number is greater.

Key idea: Among negative numbers, the one with the bigger digits is actually smaller. −9 is less than −4, just as −9°F is colder than −4°F.

Use the symbols < (is less than) and > (is greater than). The symbol always opens toward the greater number: −9 < −4.

steps: Picture both numbers on a number line. −9 is 9 units left of zero, and −4 is 4 units left of zero.

check.prompt:
Choose the phrase that makes each statement true.

−9 {{0}} −4

0 {{1}} −12

why: You compared 9 and 4 without their signs. For negative numbers the order flips: −9 is farther left on the number line, so it is less.
Two different numbers cannot be equal. −9 and −4 are different points on the number line, 5 units apart.
You compared 0 with 12 and ignored the negative sign. −12 is 12 units left of zero, so 0 is greater.
Zero and −12 are different points on the number line, 12 units apart, so they are not equal.

check.hint: Picture both numbers on a number line. The number farther to the right is greater.
check.explain:
−9 is to the left of −4 on the number line, so −9 is less than −4.

Every negative number is to the left of 0, so 0 is greater than −12.

The tempting mistake is to compare the digits only (9 > 4 and 12 > 0). With negative numbers, bigger digits mean farther below zero.

screens.title: Absolute Value and Opposites
screens.html:
The absolute value of a number is its distance from zero. Distance is never negative, so absolute value is never negative.

  • |−7| = 7 and |7| = 7. Both numbers are 7 units from zero.
  • |0| = 0.

Opposites are numbers the same distance from zero on opposite sides, like 5 and −5. A negative sign in front of a number means "the opposite of," so −(−4) = 4.

Absolute value bars also work like parentheses. Work inside them first: |3 − 11| = |−8| = 8. It is not 3 + 11.

A negative sign outside the bars stays: −|−6| = −6.

steps: |−6| = 6, and the negative sign outside the bars makes it −6.

mistakes.why: You kept the negative sign on 12. Absolute value is distance from zero, so |−12| = 12, and 12 − 5 = 7.
You added 12 and 5. The problem subtracts: |−12| − |5| = 12 − 5 = 7.

check.hint: Find each absolute value first (the distance from zero). Then subtract.
check.explain:
|−12| = 12 because −12 is 12 units from zero.

|5| = 5.

12 − 5 = 7.

If you got −17, you used −12 instead of its absolute value.

screens.title: Adding Signed Numbers
screens.html:
Think of positive numbers as money you have and negative numbers as money you owe.

  • Same signs: add the absolute values and keep the sign. −6 + (−8) = −14. (You owe 6, then owe 8 more: you owe 14.)
  • Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger one, and keep the sign of the number with the larger absolute value. −9 + 4 = −5. (You owe 9 and pay back 4: you still owe 5.)

On a number line, adding a positive number moves right, and adding a negative number moves left.

steps: The signs are different, so subtract the absolute values: 9 − 4 = 5.
The larger absolute value is 9, and −9 is negative, so the answer is negative.

mistakes.why: You subtracted correctly (15 − 8 = 7) but used the wrong sign. The number with the larger absolute value is −15, so the answer is negative.
You added 15 and 8 and kept the negative sign. That rule is for numbers with the same sign. With different signs, subtract: 15 − 8 = 7, then make it negative.
You added the absolute values and dropped the sign. With different signs, subtract the absolute values (15 − 8 = 7) and keep the sign of −15.

check.hint: The signs are different. Subtract the absolute values, then decide the sign.
check.explain:
The signs are different, so subtract the absolute values: 15 − 8 = 7.

−15 has the larger absolute value, so the answer is negative: −7.

Money check: you owe $15 and pay back $8, so you still owe $7. The tempting wrong answer, 7, has the right size but the wrong sign.

screens.title: Subtracting Signed Numbers
screens.html:
Every subtraction can be rewritten as an addition: subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite. Keep the first number, change the minus to plus, and change the sign of the second number. Then use the adding rules.

  • 6 − (−2) = 6 + 2 = 8
  • −3 − 7 = −3 + (−7) = −10
  • −8 − (−3) = −8 + 3 = −5

To find a change, such as how much a temperature rose, subtract: final value − starting value.

example.prompt: At 5 a.m. it was −7°F. By 3 p.m. it was 12°F. How many degrees did the temperature rise?
steps: Check on a number line: from −7 up to 0 is 7 degrees, and from 0 up to 12 is 12 more. 7 + 12 = 19.

mistakes.why: You computed 6 − 9. Subtracting −9 means adding 9: 6 + 9 = 15.
You added 6 and 9 but made the answer negative because of the minus signs. Subtracting a negative is adding, so 6 + 9 = 15 is positive.

check.hint: Rewrite the subtraction as adding the opposite.
check.explain:
Change the subtraction to adding the opposite: 6 − (−9) = 6 + 9.

6 + 9 = 15.

The most common mistake is 6 − 9 = −3, which ignores the negative sign on 9.

screens.title: Multiplying and Dividing Signed Numbers
screens.html:
For multiplying and dividing, the sign rules are short:

  • Same signs give a positive answer: (−4)(−5) = 20 and −24 ÷ (−6) = 4.
  • Different signs give a negative answer: (−4)(5) = −20 and 24 ÷ (−6) = −4.

With more than two factors, count the negative signs. An even number of negatives gives a positive product; an odd number gives a negative product.

These rules are only for multiplying and dividing. When you add two negatives, the answer stays negative: −3 + (−4) = −7.

Parentheses written side by side, like (−2)(5), mean multiply.

steps: Multiply without signs: 3 × 4 × 2 = 24. There are two negatives (an even number), so the product is positive: 24.
Divide without signs: 36 ÷ 4 = 9. The signs are the same, so the quotient is positive: 9.

mistakes.why: You multiplied correctly but miscounted the negatives. There are two negative factors (−2 and −3), an even number, so the product is positive.
You added the numbers (−2 + 5 − 3 = 0). Parentheses side by side mean multiply: (−2)(5)(−3).

check.hint: Multiply the numbers without their signs, then count the negative factors.
check.explain:
Multiply without signs: 2 × 5 × 3 = 30.

Count the negatives: −2 and −3 make two, an even number, so the answer is positive: 30.

Step by step: (−2)(5) = −10, and (−10)(−3) = 30. The wrong answer −30 comes from losing track of the second negative.

screens.title: Order of Operations: The Steps
screens.html:
When an expression has more than one operation, everyone follows the same order, so there is only one correct answer.

  1. Grouping symbols: parentheses ( ), brackets [ ], absolute value bars | |, and fraction bars. Work inside them first.
  2. Exponents (you will study these in Week 3).
  3. Multiplication and division, from left to right.
  4. Addition and subtraction, from left to right.

Rewrite the whole expression after each step. One step per line keeps you from losing a number or a sign.

steps: There are no grouping symbols. Multiplication comes before addition: 2 × 5 = 10.

mistakes.why: You subtracted first (20 − 8 = 12, then 12 ÷ 4 = 3). Division comes before subtraction: 8 ÷ 4 = 2, then 20 − 2 = 18.

check.hint: Which comes first, division or subtraction?
check.explain:
Division comes before subtraction: 8 ÷ 4 = 2.

20 − 2 = 18.

Working left to right (20 − 8 = 12, then 12 ÷ 4 = 3) gives 3, the most common wrong answer.

screens.title: Partners Work Left to Right
screens.html:
Many people remember the order as PEMDAS. The trap is thinking that M always comes before D and A always comes before S. They do not.

Multiplication and division are partners. Do whichever comes first, reading left to right. Addition and subtraction are partners too.

  • 24 ÷ 4 × 3 = 6 × 3 = 18 (not 24 ÷ 12 = 2)
  • 10 − 4 + 3 = 6 + 3 = 9 (not 10 − 7 = 3)

steps: Multiply and divide from left to right. The division comes first here: 12 ÷ 3 = 4, so the expression is 30 − 4 × 2.

mistakes.why: You multiplied before dividing (4 × 3 = 12, 36 ÷ 12 = 3, then 3 − 10 + 2 = −5). The division comes first here because it is on the left: 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
You added before subtracting (10 + 2 = 12, then 27 − 12 = 15). The subtraction comes first here because it is on the left: 27 − 10 = 17, then 17 + 2 = 19.

check.hint: Do multiplication and division from left to right. Then do addition and subtraction from left to right.
check.explain:
Multiply and divide, left to right: 36 ÷ 4 = 9, then 9 × 3 = 27. The expression is now 27 − 10 + 2.

Add and subtract, left to right: 27 − 10 = 17, then 17 + 2 = 19.

If you got 15, you added 10 + 2 before subtracting. If you got −5, you multiplied 4 × 3 before dividing.

screens.title: Grouping Symbols and Absolute Value
screens.html:
Grouping symbols tell you what to do first. Parentheses ( ), brackets [ ], absolute value bars | |, and the bar of a fraction all group.

  • When grouping symbols are nested, work from the inside out.
  • Inside any group, follow the normal order of operations.
  • A number written right next to a grouping symbol means multiply: 3|2 − 7| means 3 × |2 − 7|.

A fraction bar groups the top and the bottom. In (12 + 6) / (2 − 5), find 18 and −3 first, then divide: 18 ÷ (−3) = −6.

steps: Inside the brackets, multiply first: (−3)(4) = −12. Then −12 + 18 = 6.
Now the expression is 6 ÷ (−2) − |−5|. Absolute value: |−5| = 5.

check.skill: Order of operations with absolute value

mistakes.why: You added 4 + 3 first and then multiplied by 5. Multiplication comes before addition: 3 × 5 = 15, then 4 + 15 = 19.
You used −5 instead of |−5|. Absolute value is never negative: |2 − 7| = |−5| = 5.

check.hint: Work inside the absolute value bars first. 3|…| means 3 times the absolute value.
check.explain:
Inside the bars: 2 − 7 = −5, and |−5| = 5.

Multiply: 3 × 5 = 15.

Add: 4 + 15 = 19.

The tempting wrong answer 35 comes from adding 4 + 3 before multiplying.

screens.title: Order of Operations with Negative Numbers
screens.html:
The order of operations does not change when negative numbers appear, but the signs give you more chances to slip. Two habits help:

  • Keep each sign attached to the number that follows it. In 10 − 4 × (−3), the multiplication is 4 × (−3), and the 10 waits.
  • When the last step is subtracting a negative, rewrite it as adding: 10 − (−12) = 10 + 12.

The GED often builds wrong answer choices from exactly these slips, so a choice that matches your answer is not proof that you are right. Check each line.

steps: Multiply and divide, left to right: 2 × (−4) = −8, then −8 ÷ 4 = −2. Now the expression is 7 − (−2).

mistakes.why: You subtracted 10 − 4 first and then multiplied by −3. Multiplication comes first: 4 × (−3) = −12.
You found 4 × (−3) = −12 correctly, but then computed 10 − 12. Subtracting −12 means adding 12: 10 + 12 = 22.

check.hint: Multiply first. Then rewrite subtracting a negative as adding.
check.explain:
Multiply first: 4 × (−3) = −12.

Now 10 − (−12) = 10 + 12 = 22.

If you got −2, you lost the double negative at the end. If you got −18, you subtracted before multiplying.

screens.title: Fraction Basics
screens.html:
A fraction has a numerator (the top: how many parts you have) and a denominator (the bottom: how many equal parts make one whole).

  • Equivalent fractions name the same amount. Multiply or divide the top and bottom by the same number: 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12.
  • Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by a common factor: 18/24 = 3/4 (divide both by 6).
  • A mixed number has a whole part and a fraction part. To change it to an improper fraction, multiply the whole number by the denominator, add the numerator, and keep the denominator: 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4.
  • To go back, divide: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, so 17/5 = 3 2/5.

example.prompt: Simplify 18/24, and write 2 1/4 as an improper fraction.
steps: For 2 1/4: 2 × 4 = 8, then 8 + 1 = 9, and keep the denominator 4.

check.prompt: Write 3 2/5 as an improper fraction. Type it in the form a/b, for example 9/4.

mistakes.why: You multiplied the whole number by the numerator (3 × 2 = 6) and added the denominator (6 + 5 = 11). Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator: 3 × 5 + 2 = 17.
You wrote the digits 3 and 2 side by side. The whole number 3 is 15 fifths, so 3 2/5 = 15/5 + 2/5 = 17/5.

check.hint: Multiply the whole number by the denominator, then add the numerator.
check.explain:
Multiply the whole number by the denominator: 3 × 5 = 15. That is 15 fifths in 3 wholes.

Add the numerator: 15 + 2 = 17.

Keep the denominator: 17/5.

Check: 17 ÷ 5 = 3 remainder 2, which is 3 2/5. The wrong answer 11/5 comes from multiplying 3 by the numerator instead of the denominator.

screens.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
screens.html:
You can add or subtract fractions only when they have the same denominator, because the pieces must be the same size.

  1. Find a common denominator. The least common denominator (LCD) is the smallest number that both denominators divide into evenly.
  2. Rewrite each fraction as an equivalent fraction with that denominator.
  3. Add or subtract the numerators. Keep the denominator.
  4. Simplify.

Never add or subtract the denominators. 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5; it is 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

check.prompt: Find 5/6 − 1/4. Write your answer as a fraction in simplest form.

mistakes.why: You subtracted the numerators (5 − 1 = 4) and the denominators (6 − 4 = 2). Denominators are never subtracted. Rewrite both fractions with denominator 12 first.
You subtracted the numerators but kept the 6 without rewriting 1/4. The pieces must be the same size: 5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12.

check.hint: The least common denominator of 6 and 4 is 12.
check.explain:
The LCD of 6 and 4 is 12.

5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12.

10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12. It cannot be simplified.

Subtracting tops and bottoms (5 − 1 over 6 − 4) gives 4/2 = 2, which is far too big: you cannot take something away from 5/6 and end up with 2.

screens.title: Adding and Subtracting Mixed Numbers
screens.html:
The most reliable method for mixed numbers is to change them to improper fractions first, use the usual fraction steps, and then change back.

You can also work with the whole numbers and the fractions separately. If the fraction you are subtracting is bigger than the fraction you start with, you must borrow 1 whole. For example, 4 1/3 = 3 + 1 + 1/3 = 3 4/3.

Never subtract the smaller fraction from the larger one just because it is easier. In 3 1/2 − 1 2/3, doing 2/3 − 1/2 gives the wrong answer 2 1/6.

check.prompt:
Find 4 1/3 − 1 3/4.

You may type a mixed number with a space (like 2 1/2), an improper fraction, or a decimal rounded to the hundredths.

mistakes.why: You subtracted the fractions backward (3/4 − 1/3 = 5/12) because 1/3 is smaller than 3/4. Borrow 1 whole instead, or use improper fractions: 52/12 − 21/12 = 31/12.
You borrowed 1 whole to make 16/12 but did not lower the 4 to 3. After borrowing, 4 1/3 becomes 3 16/12, and 3 16/12 − 1 9/12 = 2 7/12.

check.hint: Change both mixed numbers to improper fractions with denominator 12.
check.explain:
Change to improper fractions: 4 1/3 = 13/3 and 1 3/4 = 7/4.

LCD 12: 13/3 = 52/12 and 7/4 = 21/12.

52/12 − 21/12 = 31/12.

31 ÷ 12 = 2 remainder 7, so the answer is 2 7/12 (about 2.58).

The tempting wrong answer 3 5/12 comes from subtracting 1/3 from 3/4 instead of borrowing.

screens.title: Multiplying and Dividing Fractions
screens.html:
• Multiply: numerator times numerator, denominator times denominator. No common denominator needed. 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12 = 1/2.
  • "Of" means multiply: 2/3 of 12 = 2/3 × 12/1 = 24/3 = 8.
  • Divide: keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second fraction (use its reciprocal). 3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 3/4 × 8/3 = 24/12 = 2.
  • Change mixed numbers and whole numbers to fractions first: 3 = 3/1 and 1 1/2 = 3/2.

Dividing asks "How many of these fit into that?" Two 3/8 pieces fit into 3/4, so 3/4 ÷ 3/8 = 2.

steps: Keep 5/6, change ÷ to ×, and flip 2/3 to 3/2: 5/6 × 3/2.
Simplify by dividing the top and bottom by 3: 5/4 = 1 1/4.

mistakes.why: You multiplied 3/4 × 1/8 without flipping. To divide, flip the second fraction: 3/4 × 8/1.
You flipped the first fraction instead of the second (4/3 × 1/8 = 4/24 = 1/6). Keep the first fraction as it is and flip only the second one.

check.hint: Keep, change, flip. Flip only the second fraction.
check.explain:
Keep 3/4, change ÷ to ×, and flip 1/8 to 8/1: 3/4 × 8/1 = 24/4 = 6.

Sense check: an eighth is small, so many eighths fit into 3/4. Since 3/4 = 6/8, exactly 6 fit. The wrong answer 3/32 is tiny, a sign that you multiplied instead of dividing.

screens.title: Adding, Subtracting, and Multiplying Decimals
screens.html:
• Add or subtract: line up the decimal points and fill empty places with zeros. 20 − 9.89 becomes 20.00 − 9.89 = 10.11.
  • Multiply: multiply as if there were no decimal points. Then count the decimal places in both numbers together, and give the answer that many decimal places.

Estimate to check where the decimal point goes. 0.3 × 0.2 must be less than 0.3, so it cannot be 0.6. It is 0.06.

With money, round to two decimal places (cents) at the end.

steps: Count decimal places: 1.25 has two and 2.4 has one, three in all.
Place the point three places from the right: 3.000 = 3.

mistakes.why: You used only two decimal places. 1.5 has one and 0.04 has two, so the answer needs three: 15 × 4 = 60 becomes 0.060.
You used four decimal places. Count again: one in 1.5 plus two in 0.04 is three, so 60 becomes 0.060 = 0.06.
You multiplied 15 × 4 but did not place the decimal point. Three decimal places are needed: 0.060 = 0.06.

check.hint: Multiply 15 × 4, then count the decimal places in both numbers.
check.explain:
Multiply as whole numbers: 15 × 4 = 60.

Count decimal places: 1.5 has one and 0.04 has two, three in all.

60 with three decimal places is 0.060 = 0.06.

Estimate: 1 × 0.04 = 0.04 and 2 × 0.04 = 0.08, so the answer is between 0.04 and 0.08. That rules out 0.6 and 0.006.

screens.title: Dividing Decimals
screens.html:
To divide by a decimal, first make the divisor (the number you are dividing by) a whole number.

  1. Move the decimal point in the divisor to the right until it is a whole number.
  2. Move the decimal point in the dividend (the number being divided) the same number of places. Add zeros if you need them.
  3. Divide as usual.

This works because you multiply both numbers by the same power of 10, which does not change the answer.

Check by multiplying: the quotient times the divisor should equal the dividend.

steps: Move the point in 0.12 two places to the right to make 12.
Move the point in 3.6 two places too: 360.

mistakes.why: You moved the decimal point two places in 0.08 but only one place in 7.2 (72 ÷ 8 = 9). Move both points the same number of places: 720 ÷ 8 = 90.
You moved the point in 0.08 to make 8 but did not move the point in 7.2 (7.2 ÷ 8 = 0.9). Move both points two places: 720 ÷ 8 = 90.

check.hint: Move both decimal points two places to the right.
check.explain:
Make the divisor a whole number: 0.08 becomes 8 (two places to the right).

Move the point in the dividend the same two places: 7.2 becomes 720.

720 ÷ 8 = 90.

Check: 90 × 0.08 = 7.2. The tempting answer 9 comes from moving the point only one place in 7.2.

screens.title: Converting Fractions and Decimals
screens.html:
A fraction bar means divide. To change a fraction to a decimal, divide the numerator by the denominator: 3/8 = 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375.

To change a decimal to a fraction, read its place value and simplify: 0.35 is 35 hundredths, so 0.35 = 35/100 = 7/20.

1/21/43/41/51/81/32/3
0.50.250.750.20.125≈ 0.333≈ 0.667

Memorize these pairs. They save time on the part of the test with no calculator.

example.prompt: Write 3/8 as a decimal and 0.6 as a fraction.
steps: 3 ÷ 8: 8 goes into 30 three times (24), remainder 6; into 60 seven times (56), remainder 4; into 40 five times. So 3/8 = 0.375.

mistakes.why: You wrote the digits 5 and 8 with a decimal point. A fraction bar means divide: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625.
You divided 8 by 5. Divide the numerator by the denominator: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625.

check.hint: Divide the numerator by the denominator. You can also use 1/8 = 0.125.
check.explain:
Divide 5 by 8: 5.000 ÷ 8 = 0.625.

Or use a known pair: 1/8 = 0.125, so 5/8 = 5 × 0.125 = 0.625.

Sense check: 5/8 is a bit more than 1/2, and 0.625 is a bit more than 0.5. The wrong answer 1.6 is more than 1 whole, which cannot be true for a fraction whose top is smaller than its bottom.

screens.title: Comparing and Ordering Mixed Forms
screens.html:
To compare or order numbers written in different forms, put them all in the same form first, usually decimals. Then place them on a number line in your head.

  1. Change every fraction to a decimal. Simplify any absolute values or opposites.
  2. Separate the negatives from the positives. Every negative number is less than every positive number.
  3. Among positives, compare place by place: 0.75 < 0.80.
  4. Among negatives, the order flips: the number farther from zero is less, so −1.5 < −1.2.

Writing every decimal with the same number of places (0.8 as 0.80) makes comparing easier.

steps: Negatives: −1.5 is farther from zero, so −1.5 < −1.2.

why: You compared 0.7 and 0.65 as if they were positive: 0.70 > 0.65. For negative numbers the order flips, so −0.70 is less than −0.65.
−3/4 = −0.75 is the farthest from zero of these numbers, so it is the least, not the greatest. You may have picked the number with the largest digits.
−2/3 ≈ −0.667, which is farther from zero than −0.65. You may have rounded −2/3 to −0.6 and lost the difference.
check.hint: Change each number to a decimal with three places. The greatest negative number is the one closest to zero.
check.explain:
Convert: −3/4 = −0.750 and −2/3 ≈ −0.667. The others are −0.650 and −0.700.

All four are negative, so the greatest is the one closest to zero: −0.650.

From least to greatest: −3/4, −0.7, −2/3, −0.65. The greatest is −0.65.

The tempting wrong choice is −0.7, because 0.7 > 0.65 for positive numbers.

screens.title: Solving Multi-Step Word Problems
screens.html:
Most GED math questions are word problems. Use the same four steps every time.

  1. Read. Find exactly what the question asks for and underline it.
  2. Plan. List the steps in words. Rise, gain, deposit, refund: add. Drop, spend, withdraw, use: subtract. Of, each, per, times: multiply. Split equally, how many fit: divide.
  3. Compute. One step per line, with a label (for example, "cost of shirts").
  4. Check. Estimate, and reread the question. Did you answer what was asked, or stop one step early?

example.prompt: Tom has $85.00 in his checking account. He writes checks for $42.75 and $61.30. What is his balance now?
steps: $42.25 − $61.30 = −$19.05. The second check is larger than what is left, so the balance is negative.
example.answer: His balance is −$19.05 (he is overdrawn by $19.05).

check.prompt: A cookie recipe needs 3/4 cup of sugar per batch. Jada has 5 cups of sugar. She makes 6 batches. How many cups of sugar does she have left?

mistakes.why: That is the sugar she used (6 × 3/4 = 4 1/2 cups). The question asks how much is left: 5 − 4 1/2 = 1/2.
You subtracted the sugar for only one batch (5 − 3/4). She makes 6 batches, so first find 6 × 3/4 = 4 1/2.

check.hint: First find how much sugar 6 batches use. Then subtract that from 5.
check.explain:
Plan: find the sugar used, then the sugar left.

Sugar used: 6 × 3/4 = 18/4 = 4 1/2 cups.

Sugar left: 5 − 4 1/2 = 1/2 cup.

The answer 4 1/2 is one step short: it is the sugar used, not the sugar left.

screens.title: Summary
screens.html:
• On a number line, farther right is greater. Among negatives, the number closer to zero is greater.
  • Absolute value is distance from zero and is never negative. The bars group like parentheses.
  • Adding with the same signs: add and keep the sign. With different signs: subtract and keep the sign of the larger absolute value.
  • Subtracting means adding the opposite: a − (−b) = a + b.
  • Multiplying or dividing: same signs give a positive; different signs give a negative.
  • Order of operations: grouping, exponents, multiply and divide left to right, add and subtract left to right.

6 1/4 cubic yards is the amount used. The question asks how much is left: 8 1/6 − 6 1/4.

items.hint: Add the two days first. Then subtract from 8 1/6 using a common denominator of 12. You will need to borrow.
items.explain:
Used: 2 3/4 + 3 1/2 = 2 3/4 + 3 2/4 = 5 5/4 = 6 1/4 cubic yards.

Left: 8 1/6 − 6 1/4. With a common denominator of 12: 8 2/12 − 6 3/12.

3/12 is more than 2/12, so borrow 1 whole: 8 2/12 = 7 14/12.

7 14/12 − 6 3/12 = 1 11/12 cubic yards (about 1.92).

Check with improper fractions: 98/12 − 75/12 = 23/12. The tempting wrong answer 2 1/12 comes from subtracting the fractions backward instead of borrowing.

items.prompt: A food bank has a 22.5-pound bag of rice. Volunteers have already given out 4.5 pounds. They pack the rest into small bags that hold 0.75 pound each. How many small bags can they fill?

mistakes.why: You divided the whole bag: 22.5 ÷ 0.75 = 30. They already gave out 4.5 pounds, so divide only what is left: 18 ÷ 0.75.
You moved the decimal point two places in 0.75 but only one place in 18 (180 ÷ 75 = 2.4). Move both points two places: 1,800 ÷ 75 = 24.
You moved the point in 0.75 to make 75 but did not move the point in 18 (18 ÷ 75 = 0.24). Move both points two places: 1,800 ÷ 75 = 24.

items.hint: First find how much rice is left. Then divide by the size of one small bag.
items.explain:
Rice left: 22.5 − 4.5 = 18 pounds.

Number of bags: 18 ÷ 0.75. Move both decimal points two places: 1,800 ÷ 75 = 24.

Check: 24 × 0.75 = 18. The tempting wrong answer 30 comes from dividing the whole 22.5 pounds and forgetting the rice already given out.

items.prompt: Simplify 20 − 4(3 − 8) ÷ 2. What number do you get?
why: You found 4(−5) ÷ 2 = −10 but then computed 20 − 10. Subtracting −10 means adding 10. (You also get 10 if you wrote 3 − 8 as 5.)
You subtracted 20 − 4 first and then multiplied: 16 × (−5) ÷ 2 = −40. Multiplication and division come before subtraction.
You divided the whole expression by 2: (20 + 20) ÷ 2 = 20. The ÷ 2 applies only to 4(−5), not to the 20.
items.hint: Start inside the parentheses. A number written right next to parentheses means multiply.
items.explain:
Parentheses first: 3 − 8 = −5, so the expression is 20 − 4(−5) ÷ 2

Multiply and divide from left to right:

4(−5) = −20, so 20 − (−20) ÷ 2

−20 ÷ 2 = −10, so 20 − (−10)

Subtracting a negative means adding: 20 + 10 = 30

The choice 10 comes from a sign error (20 − 10). The choice −40 comes from subtracting 20 − 4 first: 16 × (−5) ÷ 2 = −40. The choice 20 comes from dividing the whole expression, 40, by 2.

items.prompt:
Priya has a roll of ribbon that is 12 1/2 yards long. She cuts 4 pieces, and each piece is 2 2/3 yards long. How many yards of ribbon are left?

Enter your answer as a fraction, a mixed number (like 2 1/2), or a decimal rounded to the hundredths.

mistakes.why: You subtracted only one piece (12 1/2 − 2 2/3). She cuts 4 pieces, so first multiply: 4 × 2 2/3 = 10 2/3.
You multiplied only the whole number part (4 × 2 = 8) and kept the 2/3, getting 8 2/3. Change 2 2/3 to 8/3 first: 4 × 8/3 = 32/3 = 10 2/3.
10 2/3 yards is the total length cut. The question asks how much ribbon is left: 12 1/2 − 10 2/3.

items.hint: First find the total length of the 4 pieces. Then subtract that from 12 1/2.
items.explain:
Change the mixed numbers to improper fractions: 2 2/3 = 8/3 and 12 1/2 = 25/2.

Total cut: 4 × 8/3 = 32/3 = 10 2/3 yards.

Left: 25/2 − 32/3. With a common denominator of 6: 75/6 − 64/6 = 11/6.

11/6 = 1 5/6 yards (about 1.83).

If you subtract only one piece (12 1/2 − 2 2/3), you get 9 5/6 yards, which is not what the question asks.

items.prompt: Jordan earns $18.40 per hour. Last week he worked 32 1/2 hours. His employer withholds 1/4 of his pay for taxes and other deductions. How much is Jordan's take-home pay for the week?
why: $149.50 is the amount withheld (1/4 of $598.00), not the amount he keeps. He takes home 3/4 of his pay.
$598.00 is his pay before deductions. Subtract the 1/4 that is withheld.
You used 32 hours instead of 32 1/2 ($18.40 × 32 = $588.80, and 3/4 of that is $441.60). Include the half hour.
items.hint: Find his total pay first. If 1/4 is withheld, what fraction does he keep?
items.explain:
Total pay: 32 1/2 hours = 32.5 hours

$18.40 × 32.5:

$18.40 × 32 = $588.80 and $18.40 × 0.5 = $9.20

$588.80 + $9.20 = $598.00

If 1/4 is withheld, Jordan keeps 1 − 1/4 = 3/4 of his pay:

3/4 × $598.00 = $598.00 ÷ 4 × 3 = $149.50 × 3 = $448.50

$149.50 is the amount withheld, not the amount he keeps. $598.00 is his pay before deductions. $441.60 comes from leaving out the half hour (using 32 hours instead of 32.5).

items.prompt: Which list shows the numbers in order from least to greatest?
why: You ordered the negatives as if they were positive (0.25 < 0.3), so you put −1/4 first. For negatives the order flips: −0.3 is farther from zero, so it is less than −0.25.
You placed 1/8 after 0.2, maybe because 8 looks like a big digit. 1/8 = 0.125, which is less than 0.2.
You ordered the numbers by their distance from zero and ignored the signs. Every negative number is less than every positive number.
items.hint: Change the fractions to decimals first.
items.explain:
Convert to decimals: −1/4 = −0.25 and 1/8 = 0.125.

Negatives: −0.30 is farther from zero than −0.25, so −0.3 < −1/4.

Positives: 0.125 < 0.200, so 1/8 < 0.2.

Order: −0.3, −1/4, 1/8, 0.2.

The most tempting wrong list puts −1/4 first, which forgets that the order flips for negative numbers.

items.prompt: Find (−3)(−4) ÷ (−6) + 5.

mistakes.why: A sign slip made the quotient +2 instead of −2. (−3)(−4) = +12, and 12 ÷ (−6) has different signs, so it is −2. Then −2 + 5 = 3.
You added (−6) + 5 = −1 before dividing, then 12 ÷ (−1) = −12. Division comes before addition: 12 ÷ (−6) = −2 first.

items.hint: Multiply and divide from left to right, keeping track of the signs. Add last.
items.explain:
Multiply: (−3)(−4) = 12 (same signs, positive).

Divide: 12 ÷ (−6) = −2 (different signs, negative).

Add: −2 + 5 = 3.

The tempting wrong answer 7 comes from a sign slip that makes the quotient +2.

items.skill: Order of operations with absolute value
items.prompt: Evaluate 10 − 2|3 − 7| × 3.

mistakes.why: You subtracted 10 − 2 first and then multiplied: 8 × 4 × 3 = 96. Multiplication comes before subtraction.
You used −4 instead of |−4|: 10 − 2(−4)(3) = 10 + 24 = 34. Absolute value is never negative, so |3 − 7| = 4.
You computed 24 − 10 instead of 10 − 24. Taking 24 away from 10 goes below zero: −14.

items.hint: Work inside the absolute value bars first. Then multiply. Subtract last.
items.explain:
Inside the bars: 3 − 7 = −4, and |−4| = 4.

Multiply, left to right: 2 × 4 = 8, then 8 × 3 = 24.

Subtract: 10 − 24 = −14.

The tempting wrong answer 96 comes from subtracting 10 − 2 before multiplying.

items.prompt: What is 2 1/3 ÷ 1 1/6?
why: You flipped the first fraction instead of the second (3/7 × 7/6 = 1/2). Keep 7/3 as it is and flip only the divisor, 7/6.
You multiplied instead of dividing (7/3 × 7/6 = 49/18 = 2 13/18). To divide, flip the second fraction first.
You divided the whole numbers (2 ÷ 1 = 2) and the fractions (1/3 ÷ 1/6 = 2) separately and added the results. Change both mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
items.hint: Change both mixed numbers to improper fractions. Then keep, change, flip.
items.explain:
Change to improper fractions: 2 1/3 = 7/3 and 1 1/6 = 7/6.

Keep, change, flip: 7/3 × 6/7 = 42/21 = 2.

Check: 2 × 1 1/6 = 2 2/6 = 2 1/3, so 1 1/6 fits into 2 1/3 exactly twice.

The answer 2 13/18 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

items.prompt:
Cheese costs $6.40 per pound. Marcus buys 0.75 pound. How much does he pay?

Enter the amount in dollars.

mistakes.why: You counted only the two decimal places in 0.75. Count both factors: 6.4 × 0.75 has three decimal places, so 64 × 75 = 4,800 becomes 4.800 = $4.80. Less than 1 pound must cost less than $6.40.
You placed the decimal point one place too far to the left. 6.4 × 0.75 has three decimal places: 4,800 becomes 4.800 = $4.80.
You added $6.40 + 0.75. The price is per pound, so multiply: $6.40 × 0.75.

items.hint: "Per pound" means multiply. Count the decimal places in both numbers.
items.explain:
"Per pound" means multiply: $6.40 × 0.75.

Multiply as whole numbers: 64 × 75 = 4,800.

Decimal places: 6.4 has one and 0.75 has two, three in all: 4.800 = $4.80.

Check another way: 0.75 is 3/4, and 3/4 of $6.40 is $6.40 ÷ 4 × 3 = $1.60 × 3 = $4.80.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

As a decimal, 7/8 = {{0}}.

So 7/8 {{1}} 0.9.

why: You wrote the digits 7 and 8 with a decimal point. A fraction bar means divide: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875.
You divided 8 by 7. Divide the numerator by the denominator: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875.
You may have compared 875 with 9 as whole numbers, so the longer number looked bigger. Compare place by place: 0.875 has 8 tenths and 0.9 has 9 tenths, so 0.875 is less.
You may have rounded 0.875 to 0.9. The exact values are different: 0.875 < 0.900.

items.hint: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Then compare the decimals place by place.
items.explain:
7 ÷ 8 = 0.875. (You can also use 1/8 = 0.125, so 7/8 = 7 × 0.125 = 0.875.)

Compare 0.875 with 0.900: 8 tenths is less than 9 tenths, so 7/8 is less than 0.9.

The tempting mistake is to think 0.875 is greater because it has more digits.

items.prompt: A freezer is set to −18°C. During a power outage, the temperature inside rises 2.5°C each hour for 4 hours. After the power returns, the temperature drops 1.5°C each hour for 3 hours. What is the temperature inside the freezer then?
why: You added the drop instead of subtracting it: −8 + 4.5 = −3.5. A drop means subtract: −8 − 4.5 = −12.5.
You subtracted the rise: −18 − 10 − 4.5 = −32.5. A rise in temperature means add.
You started at positive 18 instead of −18 (18 + 10 − 4.5 = 23.5). The freezer starts below zero.
items.hint: Find the total rise and the total drop first. Rise means add; drop means subtract.
items.explain:
Total rise: 4 × 2.5 = 10 degrees. −18 + 10 = −8°C.

Total drop: 3 × 1.5 = 4.5 degrees. −8 − 4.5 = −12.5°C.

Sense check: it rose 10 degrees and fell 4.5, a net rise of 5.5 from −18, which gives −12.5. The choice −3.5 comes from adding the drop instead of subtracting it.

items.prompt:
A family's monthly take-home income is $3,600. They spend 1/3 of it on rent and 1/4 of it on food. How much money is left for everything else?

Enter the amount in dollars.

mistakes.why: That is the amount spent on rent and food ($1,200 + $900). The question asks how much is left: $3,600 − $2,100.
You subtracted only the rent ($3,600 − $1,200). Subtract the food too: 1/4 of $3,600 is $900.
You added the fractions by adding tops and bottoms (1/3 + 1/4 = 2/7). With a common denominator, 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12, so 5/12 is left.

items.hint: Find 1/3 of $3,600 and 1/4 of $3,600. Then subtract both from $3,600.
items.explain:
Rent: 1/3 of $3,600 = $3,600 ÷ 3 = $1,200.

Food: 1/4 of $3,600 = $3,600 ÷ 4 = $900.

Left: $3,600 − $1,200 − $900 = $1,500.

Another way: they spend 1/3 + 1/4 = 4/12 + 3/12 = 7/12, so 5/12 is left, and 5/12 of $3,600 = $300 × 5 = $1,500. The tempting wrong answer $2,100 is the amount spent, not the amount left.

items.prompt: Which list shows the numbers in order from least to greatest?
why: You ordered the negatives as if they were positive (0.6 < 0.667), so you put −0.6 first. For negatives the order flips: −2/3 ≈ −0.667 is farther from zero, so it is less.
You placed 5/8 after 0.7, maybe by comparing the 8 with the 7. 5/8 = 0.625, which is less than 0.7.
You ordered the numbers by their distance from zero (0.6, 0.625, 0.667, 0.7) and ignored the signs. Every negative number is less than every positive number.
items.hint: Change the fractions to decimals first.
items.explain:
Convert to decimals: −2/3 ≈ −0.667 and 5/8 = 0.625.

Negatives: −0.667 is farther from zero than −0.600, so −2/3 < −0.6.

Positives: 0.625 < 0.700, so 5/8 < 0.7.

Order: −2/3, −0.6, 5/8, 0.7.

The most tempting wrong list puts −0.6 first, which forgets that the order flips for negative numbers.

items.prompt: Find −20 ÷ (−4) × (−3) − 2.

mistakes.why: You made 5 × (−3) positive. Different signs multiply to a negative: −15. Then −15 − 2 = −17.
You found −15 correctly but then computed −15 + 2. Subtracting 2 moves farther left: −15 − 2 = −17.

items.hint: Divide and multiply from left to right, keeping track of the signs. Subtract last.
items.explain:
Divide: −20 ÷ (−4) = 5 (same signs, positive).

Multiply: 5 × (−3) = −15 (different signs, negative).

Subtract: −15 − 2 = −17.

The tempting wrong answer −13 comes from moving the wrong way at the last step.

items.skill: Order of operations with absolute value
items.prompt: Evaluate 7 + 4|1 − 6| ÷ 2.

mistakes.why: You added 7 + 4 first: 11 × 5 ÷ 2 = 27.5. Multiplication and division come before addition.
You used −5 instead of |−5|: 7 + 4(−5) ÷ 2 = 7 − 10 = −3. Absolute value is never negative, so |1 − 6| = 5.

items.hint: Work inside the absolute value bars first. Then multiply and divide. Add last.
items.explain:
Inside the bars: 1 − 6 = −5, and |−5| = 5.

Multiply and divide, left to right: 4 × 5 = 20, then 20 ÷ 2 = 10.

Add: 7 + 10 = 17.

The tempting wrong answer 27.5 comes from adding 7 + 4 before multiplying.

items.prompt: What is 3 3/4 ÷ 1 1/4?
why: You flipped the first fraction instead of the second (4/15 × 5/4 = 1/3). Keep 15/4 as it is and flip only the divisor, 5/4.
You multiplied instead of dividing (15/4 × 5/4 = 75/16 = 4 11/16). To divide, flip the second fraction first.
You divided the whole numbers (3 ÷ 1 = 3) and the fractions (3/4 ÷ 1/4 = 3) separately and added the results. Change both mixed numbers to improper fractions first.
items.hint: Change both mixed numbers to improper fractions. Then keep, change, flip.
items.explain:
Change to improper fractions: 3 3/4 = 15/4 and 1 1/4 = 5/4.

Keep, change, flip: 15/4 × 4/5 = 60/20 = 3.

Check: 3 × 1 1/4 = 3 3/4, so 1 1/4 fits into 3 3/4 exactly three times.

The answer 4 11/16 comes from multiplying instead of dividing.

items.prompt:
Sliced turkey costs $7.20 per pound. Nadia buys 0.65 pound. How much does she pay?

Enter the amount in dollars.

mistakes.why: You counted only the two decimal places in 0.65. Count both factors: 7.2 × 0.65 has three decimal places, so 72 × 65 = 4,680 becomes 4.680 = $4.68. Less than 1 pound must cost less than $7.20.
You placed the decimal point one place too far to the left. 7.2 × 0.65 has three decimal places: 4,680 becomes 4.680 = $4.68.
You added $7.20 + 0.65. The price is per pound, so multiply: $7.20 × 0.65.

items.hint: "Per pound" means multiply. Count the decimal places in both numbers.
items.explain:
"Per pound" means multiply: $7.20 × 0.65.

Multiply as whole numbers: 72 × 65 = 4,680.

Decimal places: 7.2 has one and 0.65 has two, three in all: 4.680 = $4.68.

Check another way: $7.20 × 0.5 = $3.60 and $7.20 × 0.15 = $1.08, so $3.60 + $1.08 = $4.68. The tempting wrong answer $46.80 comes from counting only the decimal places in 0.65.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

As a decimal, 3/5 = {{0}}.

So 3/5 {{1}} 0.58.

why: You wrote the digits 3 and 5 with a decimal point. A fraction bar means divide: 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.
You divided 5 by 3. Divide the numerator by the denominator: 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.
You may have compared 6 with 58 as whole numbers, so 0.58 looked bigger. Compare place by place: 0.60 has 6 tenths and 0.58 has 5 tenths, so 0.6 is greater.
You may have rounded 0.58 to 0.6. The exact values are different: 0.60 > 0.58.

items.hint: Divide the numerator by the denominator. Then compare the decimals place by place.
items.explain:
3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. (3/5 = 6/10.)

Compare 0.60 with 0.58: 6 tenths is more than 5 tenths, so 3/5 is greater than 0.58.

The tempting mistake is to think 0.58 is greater because 58 is bigger than 6. Write 0.6 as 0.60 to compare.

items.prompt: Dario's checking account balance is −$42.50 (he is overdrawn). He deposits 3 paychecks of $125.40 each. Then he pays $210.75 for rent. What is his balance now?
why: You started at positive $42.50 instead of −$42.50 ($42.50 + $376.20 − $210.75 = $207.95). Being overdrawn means the balance is below zero.
You added only one paycheck (−$42.50 + $125.40 − $210.75 = −$127.85). He deposits 3 paychecks: 3 × $125.40 = $376.20.
$333.70 is his balance after the deposits but before rent. Subtract the rent: $333.70 − $210.75 = $122.95.
items.hint: Find the total of the deposits first. Deposits add; payments subtract. Start at −$42.50.
items.explain:
Deposits: 3 × $125.40 = $376.20.

After deposits: −$42.50 + $376.20 = $333.70.

After rent: $333.70 − $210.75 = $122.95.

The tempting wrong answer $207.95 comes from treating the starting balance as positive.

items.prompt: A delivery van has a 24-gallon gas tank. At the start of the day the tank is 3/4 full. By the end of the day, the van has used 2/3 of the gas that was in the tank at the start. How many gallons are left?

mistakes.why: That is the gas used (2/3 of 18 gallons). The question asks how much is left: 18 − 12 = 6.
You took 2/3 of the full 24-gallon tank (16 gallons) and got 24 − 16 = 8. The van used 2/3 of the gas that was in the tank, which was 3/4 of 24 = 18 gallons.
That is the gas at the start of the day (3/4 of 24). Subtract the gas used: 2/3 of 18 = 12.

items.hint: First find how much gas was in the tank at the start. Then find 2/3 of that amount.
items.explain:
Gas at the start: 3/4 of 24 = 24 ÷ 4 × 3 = 18 gallons.

Gas used: 2/3 of 18 = 18 ÷ 3 × 2 = 12 gallons.

Gas left: 18 − 12 = 6 gallons.

The tempting wrong answer 12 is the gas used, not the gas left.

vocab.def: A whole number or its opposite; integers have no fraction or decimal part.
A number less than zero; it sits to the left of zero on the number line.
vocab.example: A temperature of −8°F is 8 degrees below zero.

vocab.def: A straight line with numbers placed in order; numbers increase to the right.
vocab.example: −3 is to the left of 1, so −3 < 1.

vocab.def: The number the same distance from zero on the other side of zero.
vocab.example: The opposite of 6 is −6; the opposite of −2 is 2.

vocab.def: A number's distance from zero; it is never negative. Written with bars | |.
The agreed order for doing steps: grouping symbols, exponents, multiplication and division left to right, then addition and subtraction left to right.
The top number of a fraction; it tells how many parts you have.
The bottom number of a fraction; it tells how many equal parts make one whole.
A shared denominator that lets you add or subtract fractions.
Fractions that name the same amount.
A whole number together with a fraction.
A fraction whose numerator is greater than or equal to its denominator.
A fraction flipped upside down; a number times its reciprocal equals 1. Used to divide fractions.
The value of a digit based on its position in a number.
vocab.example: In 4.375, the 7 is in the hundredths place.

vocab.def: The smallest number that two or more denominators all divide into evenly.

notes:
Week 1 Study Sheet: Number Sense

Integer Sign Rules

OperationRuleExample
Add, same signsAdd; keep the sign−5 + (−3) = −8
Add, different signsSubtract; keep sign of larger absolute value−9 + 4 = −5
SubtractAdd the opposite6 − (−2) = 8
Multiply/divide, same signsPositive(−4)(−5) = 20
Multiply/divide, different signsNegative−24 ÷ 6 = −4

Many factors: even number of negatives → positive; odd → negative.

Absolute value = distance from 0: |−7| = 7. Farther right on the number line = greater: −2 > −5.

Order of Operations

  1. Grouping: ( ), [ ], | |, fraction bars
  2. Exponents
  3. Multiply and divide, left to right
  4. Add and subtract, left to right

30 − 12 ÷ 3 × 2 = 30 − 4 × 2 = 30 − 8 = 22

7 − 2 × (5 − 9) ÷ 4 = 7 − (−8) ÷ 4 = 7 − (−2) = 9

Fractions

  • Add/subtract: common denominator, then combine numerators.
  • Multiply: top × top, bottom × bottom. "Of" means multiply.
  • Divide: keep, change, flip.
  • Mixed to improper: 2 1/4 = (2 × 4 + 1)/4 = 9/4.
  • Always simplify.

Decimals

  • Add/subtract: line up decimal points.
  • Multiply: count total decimal places.
  • Divide: make the divisor a whole number; move both points the same way.
  • Fraction to decimal: top ÷ bottom.
  • Compare: write in one form; for negatives the order flips.

Common Fraction-Decimal Pairs

Word problems: Read (underline the question), Plan (list the steps), Compute (one step per line), Check (estimate; did you answer what was asked?).

Top mistakes: working only left to right; 5 − (−3) is 8, not 2; never add denominators; count decimal places when multiplying; work inside absolute value bars first; reread the question so you do not stop one step early.
